title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
summary:
JioHotstar evaluated 6 approaches to code retrieval for AI coding agents using SWE, CodeScale Bench, and an internal question-answering harness. Structural search performed well on concrete tasks, while semantic retrieval helped with ambiguous requirements. The findings highlight trade-offs in accuracy, token use, and tool design, underscoring the need to match retrieval tools to task types.

By Leela Kumili

title: Introducing new AI functions for AlloyDB: ai.classify and ai.extract
summary:
Transactional databases store vast amounts of unstructured text — clinical notes, customer reviews, support tickets, invoices, and property descriptions. Historically, working with this text meant building complex application code: You had to export data from the database, call external model endpoints, write custom prompt wrappers, parse unpredictable responses, manage retry logic, and update database records. This application-side loop creates operational friction. It introduces query latency, bloats application code, increases model token costs, and creates data compliance risks by moving sensitive information across multiple network boundaries.

We built AlloyDB AI to bring Gemini world knowledge directly into your operational database. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a disconnected external service, we integrated model intelligence directly into the database engine. Today, we are announcing the preview of two new SQL functions in the AlloyDB AI query engine — ai.classify and ai.extract — available in the google_ml_integration extension (version 1.6.1 or later) on PostgreSQL 18, allowing you to perform classification and structured extraction directly inside your database using standard SQL. Supported by smart batching for AI functions (previously known as AI Function Acceleration), these functions deliver production scalability and performance. 

Now, let’s take a look at these new functions and how to use them.

Classifying text directly in SQL with ai.classify

The ai.classify function categorizes text into user-defined classes without requiring manual prompt engineering. You can specify categories as a simple list of labels or provide a list containing label names and descriptions to guide model context.

Key capabilities include:

  • Single-label classification (output_mode => 'single') to assign the single best category

  • Multi-label classification (output_mode => 'multi') to return all matching categories

  • Category descriptions using 2D arrays to provide explicit context for each label

  • Few-shot prompting by supplying inline examples

  • Flexible execution modes for individual rows (TEXT), arrays (TEXT[]), and cursors (REFCURSOR)

Here’s a quick example showing how you can classify customer feedback directly within a SQL query:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nCREATE TABLE product_reviews (id INT, review TEXT);\r\n\r\nINSERT INTO product_reviews VALUES\r\n(1, 'Fantastic, would buy again!'),\r\n(2, 'Broken on arrival.'),\r\n(3, 'Mediocre, not worth the price.');\r\n\r\nSELECT unnest(\r\n ai.classify(\r\n inputs => ARRAY(SELECT review FROM product_reviews ORDER BY id),\r\n categories => ARRAY[\r\n ['positive', 'Good sentiment'],\r\n ['neutral', 'Neither good nor bad sentiment'],\r\n ['negative', 'Bad sentiment']\r\n ],\r\n batch_size => 5\r\n )\r\n) AS sentiment;\r\n\r\n-- Expected Output:\r\n-- sentiment\r\n-- ---------\r\n-- positive\r\n-- negative\r\n-- negative"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55dfa74a90>)])]>

Extracting structured JSON with ai.extract

The ai.extract function transforms unstructured text into structured JSON data matching your target schema — specified as a JSON schema or a text list of fields. It handles system instructions internally, saving you from writing prompt templates or response parsers.

Key capabilities include:

  • Schema flexibility supporting standard JSON schemas or plain text field lists

  • Automatic transformation of unstructured text into machine-readable JSON

  • Overloaded function signatures for single rows, arrays, and cursor batching

Here’s an example extracting clinical fields from free-form medical notes:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nSELECT ai.extract( \r\n input => \'Patient Jane Smith, 52 years old, visited the clinic on Oct 25. She is currently experiencing a mild fever, persistent cough, and severe body aches. The doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and Amoxicillin.\',\r\n output_schema => \'{\r\n "patient_name": {"type": "string"},\r\n "age": {"type": "integer"},\r\n "symptoms": {\r\n "type": "array",\r\n "items": {"type": "string"}\r\n },\r\n "prescribed_medications": {\r\n "type": "array",\r\n "items": {"type": "string"}\r\n }\r\n }\'\r\n);\r\n\r\n--- Expected output \r\n-- {\r\n-- "patient_name": "Jane Smith",\r\n-- "age": 52,\r\n-- "symptoms": [\r\n-- "mild fever",\r\n-- "persistent cough",\r\n-- "severe body aches"\r\n-- ],\r\n-- "prescribed_medications": [\r\n-- "Ibuprofen",\r\n-- "Amoxicillin"\r\n-- ]\r\n-- }'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55eaeb7410>)])]>

Speeding up queries with smart batching

Running AI evaluations row-by-row can slow down query execution. AlloyDB addresses this with smart batching for AI functions. When you use ai.classify or ai.extract in SQL WHERE clause expressions, the database engine automatically groups inputs into optimized micro-batches before sending them to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models.

Smart batching delivers significant performance and efficiency improvements:

  • Faster inference for query execution compared to row-at-a-time evaluations

  • Reduces total model token spend by optimizing input prompt overhead

Real-world industry applications

Native classification and extraction functions support operational workflows across key industry sectors:

  • Healthcare: Securely convert free-text clinical notes into structured records containing patient names, symptoms, and prescribed medications, keeping patient data safely within the confines of the database.

  • Financial services: Extract vendor details, invoice dates, and line-item totals from scanned document text.

  • Legal technology: Pull governing law, liability caps, and termination notice periods from contract documents.

  • Real estate: Extract property types, bedroom counts, and price ranges from descriptive listing text.

  • Knowledge graphs: Extract entities and relationships from documents to populate PostgreSQL Property Graph (PGQ) structures.

Next steps and getting started

We are continuing to expand in-database AI capabilities in AlloyDB, with upcoming enhancements planned for advanced cost optimization, line-level provenance tracking, and query pushdowns beyond WHERE clauses.

To start using ai.classify and ai.extract in your database:

  • Review the AlloyDB AI Query Engine documentation.

  • Explore the AlloyDB release notes.

title: Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions
summary: Meet the Gemini Decisions API, powered by our state-of-the-art model Gemini Decision for fast, calibrated multimodal decisions.
story_key: model:gemini|title:gemini decisions api fast calibrated multimodal decisions
content_excerpt: Introducing the Gemini Decisions API, powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model. Evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a fast, single pass across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. We are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides. Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio . The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed. On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error. Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API. Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost. title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
summary:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

title: How our GTM Agent builds consistent, high-quality sales artifacts
summary: Learn how LangChain built GTM Agent on Deep Agents to build high-quality, custom sales artifacts trained on business context.
story_key: story|title:how our gtm agent builds consistent high quality sales artifacts
content_excerpt: Over the last 12 weeks, our internal GTM Agent has saved LangChain's sales reps thousands of hours across its workflows. In that time, it generated 1,540 sales artifacts, which reps used to build by hand, one account at a time. These artifacts include customized account plans, proof-of-value documents, proposal decks, and onboarding plans. A powerful model can speed up artifact creation, one of the biggest time sinks in any deal, but can only take automation so far. What makes the biggest difference is everything built around the model: This post walks through how we used business context to build artifact generation with our GTM agent, and how we shaped it to fit the way LangChain sells. You can replicate this work on top of the Deep Agents harness. The primitives it depends on (a sandbox, skills, memory, and scheduled runs) are available in our managed version, Managed Deep Agents , so a team building something similar can get straight to capturing how its business runs. Earlier this year we wrote about how we built LangChain’s GTM Agent , which now runs a wide range of our sales and marketing workflows. It researches new leads and drafts personalized outreach for reps to approve in Slack, and every week it surfaces account signals like expansion opportunities and deal risks. Since reps were already using it every day, it was the natural place to take on one of the most time-consuming parts of their job: building sales collateral. That work was overdue for a fix. Inconsistent versions of the same document were showing up across the org. Account executives built proposal decks by pulling usage data into a chat assistant and assembling the deck themselves. The same work got repeated on every deal, and it looked different every time. We needed a way to standardize our hard-won lessons on what works without slowing anyone down. The third goal was the hardest to get right. Every stage of a deal has gates, or things that must happen before the deal can move forward, like naming an economic buyer or agreeing on success criteria. We track which stage every deal is in and which artifact helps clear each gate. But when this work was all manual, a skipped step usually came to light in a pipeline review, weeks after the rep could have asked the customer. Now that artifacts are filed through the GTM Agent, it can spot a missing one while the deal is still active. This workflow also gives our sales leaders a natural place to weigh in. They can tell us what is working

title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
summary: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. However, existing methods primarily represent skills as natural language documents, intertwining procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and making skills difficult to maintain and evolve. To address this limitation, we propose PASE (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution), a program-aided framework that iteratively evolves skills by associating them with executable programs. Unlike prior approaches that encode trajectory-derived experience primarily in natural language, PASE separates reusable procedural logic into editable programs, enabling targeted updates to executable components while reducing the need to repeatedly revise natural language skills. Extensive experiments across diverse models and benchmarks demonstrate that PASE consistently outperforms all baselines, by achieving over 2.8% improvements. Further analyses show that PASE exhibits greater evolutionary stability and generalisation capability, highlighting the critical role of programmatic knowledge in skill evolution. We will release all data and code via GitHub.

title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
summary: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

title: Announcing GA of Genie Ontology
summary: AI agents are only as useful as their understanding of the business in which they work. Within a given domain...
story_key: story|title:announcing ga of genie ontology
content_excerpt: The agentic ontology, built by agents, governed by people, and designed for every agent, is now Generally Available with expanded knowledge sources and new tools to curate and refine it. AI agents are only as useful as their understanding of the business in which they work. Within a given domain, teams can curate that understanding by hand. Thousands of customers now run Genie Agents in production this way, including 7-Eleven, Virgin Atlantic and General Motors. However, enterprises are no longer deploying a single agent for a single domain. They are deploying many agents across every function, and each needs the same accurate and complete understanding of how the business works. The enterprise context that agents need is far larger than any team can write down or model by hand. It lives in the logic behind thousands of production dashboards, SQL queries, notebooks and BI semantic models, as well as in the documents and applications where teams record definitions and maintain a working knowledge of who does what. It also changes every week as products launch, campaigns run, and teams reorganize. This is why ontologies have historically struggled in the enterprise. Built by specialists and maintained manually, they captured only a narrow slice of the business and quickly became outdated as the business evolved. Agents change both sides of that problem. They are now the primary consumers of enterprise context, and they can also produce it by learning from the work teams already do. The result is a new kind of agentic ontology, built by agents, used by agents and governed by the people who know the business. We believe every organization will need a single agentic ontology that connects to all of its data, learns continuously from how the business operates and gives every agent the same governed understanding, whether it runs on Databricks or elsewhere. Building context, agent by agent, produces separate and partial views of the business, and those views inevitably conflict. An enterprise ontology should therefore be shared infrastructure that IT and data leaders own in the same way they own the data platform beneath it. At Data + AI Summit, we introduced Genie Ontology as that layer. Today, we're announcing its General Availability, with new sources for agents to learn from and new tools for people to curate and govern what they learn. content_excerpt: Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation
summary: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

title: Which Successes Make Good References? Action-Sequence Alignment for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-inference distribution mismatch by supervising a student on its own trajectories. For multi-turn tool-use agents, conditioning the teacher on a validated same-task successful trajectory as a reference can provide useful hindsight, but different successes may reach incompatible interaction states and offer misleading supervision. We cast successful-reference selection as a free-target optimal transport problem, which reduces to assigning each failed trajectory its most compatible successful reference. Because latent state paths are hidden, we use action-sequence alignment as an observable proxy for compatibility and instantiate it with longest common subsequence (LCS), which identifies a shared ordered backbone of actions while allowing recoverable detours. This perspective makes trajectory compatibility the central criterion for reference selection in multi-turn OPD. Experiments on ALFWorld and the airline domain of $τ^3$-bench show that LCS is the only evaluated reference selector to improve over reference-free OPD on both ALFWorld overall scores and all three airline metrics. Without further optimization, the airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain, where LCS improves all three metrics.

Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. What happens when students can one-shot last year’s homework? Inside CS146S and the engineering team at Monaco. The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. title: claude-code v2.1.319
summary:
What's changed

  • Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 turns on the server-side check even with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the 1 too
  • Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
  • Added permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
  • Added /claude-api latency-optimize to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
  • Added spend for today, this week and this month to /usage for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
  • Added admin.pooled_conflict_rule and admin.pooled_priority_order to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
  • Added an optional login_notice setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with severity, time and message, for log collectors that read the level from a field
  • Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's availableModels also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
  • Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no desktopHome that rely on coworkTabEnabled: false or chatSessionRetentionDays, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
  • Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from ant auth login, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
  • Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from ant auth login
  • Added an "Earlier in this session" row to /tasks that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
  • Added a note to /loop confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
  • Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
  • Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after --resume
  • Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named HEAD
  • Fixed /diff showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named HEAD at its top level
  • Fixed the /diff pane opening blank in sessions where 64 or more turns edited files
  • Fixed slash commands typed after a leading space, tab or newline being sent to Claude as plain text instead of running
  • Fixed a request that kept failing with a 401 refreshing your login on every retry and causing 401s in your other sessions
  • Fixed /context sending its full visual grid to Claude on every later turn; Claude now reads only the table
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 in auto mode when its actions were refused because no safety check was available: text and JSON output now exit 1
  • Fixed a case where Claude Code listed every project file at start on Linux for projects on a network file system (NFS, SMB, Lustre and similar)
  • Fixed a case where auto mode was wrongly refused when a client sent a model change and a request for auto mode back to back
  • Fixed /status showing "Auto mode server: Enabled" when the server-side review isn't reaching the session, for example behind an LLM gateway that drops it
  • Fixed Claude-drafted feedback, surveys and /feedback continuing to appear after the server refused feedback for your organization
  • Fixed Claude drafting feedback on third-party gateways, where it can't be sent
  • Fixed auto mode refusing actions without saying why when permission rules or autoMode settings are very large: it now explains and, unless autoMode deny rules are set, asks you in the terminal
  • Fixed a case where Bash deny and ask rules missed commands written with quoted words
  • Fixed subagent hand-back reports showing an internal marker and provenance note when expanded outside verbose mode
  • Fixed claude -p --resume with a prompt losing a deferred tool call when its MCP server is missing: the run now exits 1, keeps the call and refuses later input
  • Fixed a case where text was dropped from informational messages sent to SDK clients
  • Fixed a case where Agent SDK hosts got a generic exit-code error instead of a failed run's own error message when the disk was full
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a turn that was interrupted in plan mode when the session resumes in another permission mode
  • Fixed edits to a settings file being ignored when made within a few seconds of Claude Code writing that file
  • Fixed a config file left at the legacy name hiding your setup with no warning: Claude Code now says on stderr when a home holds two config files, and which is in use
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json, settings and edited files ending up empty or cut off when the disk fills during a save in a read-only folder or to a bind-mounted file (one session saving at a time)
  • Fixed Write ending the turn as a refusal when it couldn't read the file to overwrite
  • Fixed background Bash commands that finish almost instantly losing their output while being reported as completed
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files missing a file that the command wrote just before it ended
  • Fixed a mistyped model name, such as opus-5-5, telling you to update Claude Code instead of suggesting the model you meant
  • Fixed a case where NotebookEdit changed the wrong cell when the notebook changed while a permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a ~0.5s hang after pressing Enter on the /login success screen: the dialog now dismisses immediately and the post-login refresh runs in the background
  • Fixed Ctrl+G not opening the external editor while typing an "Other" answer to a question in screen reader mode
  • Fixed Monitor's WebSocket watch failing with "could not resolve" behind a proxy when CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS is set and the machine has no DNS of its own
  • Fixed claude plugin eval warnings suggesting max: 0 for a tool that must not be called, which could never pass
  • Fixed background plugin auto-update not installing a dependency added by the updated plugin version
  • Fixed Cmd+click not opening links in Ghostty over tmux in sessions opened from the agents view
  • Fixed a mod's hot reload in .claude/skills missing a file that was deleted just after it appeared, and missing its return
  • Fixed /rewind failing with "No files were restored" when restoring code to a checkpoint from before /branch
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying Console web settings don't apply to Managed Agents sessions, and tightened its credential and permission examples
  • Fixed needless permission prompts for read-only commands wrapped in a plain timeout DURATION, such as timeout 30 rg foo
  • Fixed WebFetch describing claude.ai shared-chat links as empty pages; it now says shared chats can't be read and to paste the conversation instead
  • Fixed Artifact database calls being re-sent to artifacts without a database; errors now say whether republishing helps
  • Fixed a case where artifact database reads that save to a folder (out_dir) were refused
  • Fixed detailed beta tracing not presenting CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT to collectors that require a client certificate
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry claude_code.session.count metric counting Agent SDK prewarm() processes that were never claimed; a pre-started process now counts once, when it is claimed
  • Fixed /clear killing running commands of background agents, teammates and workflows that keep running, and foreground subagents of background agents and teammates
  • Fixed a terminal whose Claude apps gateway sign-in had expired sending telemetry and managed-settings requests that the gateway refused and logged as invalid_token
  • Fixed the agents view appearing to send a reply to a background session waiting on a permission prompt; the reply now stays in the box with a hint to open the session and answer
  • Fixed agent view removing a draft saved by another agent view in the same directory when exiting
  • Fixed a case where agent view came back with another agent view's input text after restarting itself for an update
  • Fixed the agents view preview cutting off long commands, results and status lines without an ellipsis, and dropping **, backticks and tags from commands waiting for approval
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome reporting the extension as not connected when the connection dropped mid-action; Claude now checks the page before repeating an action that may have run
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions still showing "Limit reached" on other devices after a usage limit was lifted outside the session
  • Fixed the file card sometimes missing in the Claude iOS app when Claude sent a single file
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions failing with no explanation when the server keeps refusing to renew model access: the runner now retries sooner and posts a warning in the session
  • Fixed /permissions in cloud sessions replying only that it isn't available; it now says where the session's rules live and how to change them
  • Fixed cloud sessions losing session-scoped deny and ask permission rules, such as those a PermissionRequest hook adds, when the session moves to a new worker
  • Fixed mod hot-reloading turning off for the session when you typed three messages instead of answering its question in a cloud session
  • Fixed background tasks that keep running after /clear disappearing from the task list in Claude Code on the web until another task started or ended
  • Fixed hidden commands appearing in the slash command menu of cloud sessions on mobile and web
  • Fixed a case where /rewind could restore or delete a file through a directory symlink
  • Fixed a case where a sed command could skip the permission check in accept-edits and auto mode
  • Fixed a case where CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 in managed settings was ignored behind an LLM gateway when the gateway's URL is set only there and server-managed settings can't be fetched
  • Fixed a Bash permission bypass where a crafted environment prefix could hide part of a command from permission checks
  • Fixed a case where deny and ask rules, hook matchers and disallowedTools entries written with a claude.ai connector's terminal name (mcp__claude_ai_Slack) were ignored in Claude Desktop (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Fixed a sandbox escape when creating a worktree
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: --trust-workspace false now also stops hooks in the repository's settings files and skills from running
  • Fixed a case where idle background sessions started through a shell-exported LLM gateway left the gateway after an update
  • Fixed help links in /status and the auto mode billing notice opening only part of the address when they wrap
  • Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC was set. With it set, Claude Code now makes a TLS handshake with the configured API host after a certificate failure, through your http:// proxy if one is set; it sends no API request
  • Fixed claude remote-control exiting silently with status 0 when a first-run question gets no answer (scripts, services, batch jobs, Ctrl+C); it now says why and exits 1
  • Fixed claude remote-control ignoring a piped y that has no newline after it at the first-run question; it now counts as a yes
  • Fixed /rename reporting plain success when the new name could not be saved to the session transcript; it now warns that the new name may not last
  • Fixed ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} not being substituted in a plugin-provided subagentStatusLine command, which can now reference the plugin's own scripts
  • Fixed claude plugin update and /plugin "Update now" not installing dependencies added by the new plugin version
  • Fixed subagents being told after compaction to expect a completion notice for background agents they neither started nor took over
  • Fixed a case where a background agent's later report was lost silently: the notification now says it was refused and how to ask for it
  • Improved config saves on Windows: Claude Code waits longer for a file another program has open, so a kill during a save is less likely to leave ~/.claude.json empty
  • Improved Claude in Chrome after a brief disconnect: it waits up to 6 seconds for the session's own browser to return before picking another
  • Improved Claude in Chrome: javascript_tool results of up to 60,000 characters now stay in the conversation instead of being saved to a file
  • Improved claude purge and the clean-up of old sessions to retry a folder that could not be fully deleted, and to report it as an error if it remains
  • Improved the refusal for a path outside the working directories on macOS and Windows: when only its letter case differs from a path inside them, the message names that spelling
  • Improved the contrast of faint gray secondary text, such as hints, details in /stats, /model and /sandbox, and rejected-action messages
  • Improved the artifact database error when an update targets a document that does not exist, and when the service pauses repeated refused writes
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's warnings about a failed upstream call: each now names the upstream, not only its provider
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: it reads "spend limit reached · resets Dec 1", then admin.blocked_message if one is set
  • Improved the /model picker: older models are now grouped under a "More models" row instead of being listed after the current ones
  • Improved /context at the terminal so the table Claude reads stays short: each list keeps its 10 largest rows, and MCP tools that load on demand share one row per server until they're called
  • Improved /usage in cloud sessions: it now links to Settings → Usage on claude.ai in a case where plan limits can't be shown
  • [VSCode] Improved the confirmation for removing a plugin marketplace: it now checks which of its plugins are installed at that moment
  • Changed MCP tasks to work in the terminal without feature-flag fetching (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, LLM gateways, DISABLE_TELEMETRY); set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASKS=1 to turn them off
  • Changed auto mode so that a project's settings files or a plugin can no longer switch its server-side check back on once you have switched it off outside the project
  • Changed Monitor's WebSocket watch to follow a rule on every Bash command: a deny refuses it, and under an ask rule an allow on Monitor, bypass mode or auto mode no longer skips the prompt
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS so that settings files can no longer set it where the host manages the network; set it in the process environment
  • Changed a session's exact Bash or PowerShell ask rule to be refused, not asked about, when a broader deny rule covers the command
  • Changed the Bash tool to ask for permission before running which with flags outside a lookup/display set
  • Changed --add-dir directories to register plugin marketplaces only once that directory's own trust dialog has been accepted
  • Changed nested skill loading: with the Bash sandbox on, skills in .claude/skills folders below the starting folder load only if you start Claude Code there or /cd there
  • Changed self-paced /loop to end when a turn finishes without rescheduling, instead of scheduling a fallback wakeup; set CLAUDE_CODE_LOOP_KEEPALIVE=1 to keep the old behavior
  • Changed PostToolUse hooks to run, with up to 10 seconds to finish, on tool calls that finish after a new message interrupts the turn
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a subagent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed cloud sessions to drop session-scoped allow rules at a move to a new worker when their deny and ask rules can't all be kept, so you may be asked again
  • Changed the automatic certificate repair behind a TLS-inspecting proxy: it no longer runs when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy variable set. Set HTTPS_PROXY to the proxy's http:// URL instead
  • Changed artifact database saves of rows others may have written: each file gets a hidden marker file, and existing files without one, earlier versions' exports among them, are left alone and reported
  • Updated /claude-api managed-agents-onboard templates to match the Claude Console: removed Performance tuner, renamed two, and turned off web search and fetch in five whose prompts don't use them
  • Removed shortcuts_list and shortcuts_execute, which listed and started shortcuts saved in the extension, from Claude Code's built-in Claude in Chrome tools
  • Gateway: Added startup warnings for upstreams that mix AWS GovCloud with other upstreams, and for base URL variables in the gateway's environment
  • Gateway: Added a start-up log warning when managed settings name an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in a header, which the gateway doesn't forward, and no bedrock upstream sets a guardrail
  • Gateway: Fixed Claude Desktop offering a web search tool that always failed when every upstream is Amazon Bedrock
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner started with --use-anthropic-git-proxy or --configure-git registering before a failed startup check made it exit; it now exits first
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_CHECKOUT_PATH so that each repository in a session gets its own folder: a folder name already taken in the session gets -2, -3, … at the end
  • Self-hosted runner: Removed the end-of-session upload of a session's debug log; a failed session's log stays on the runner host unless --remove-session-state is set
  • [VSCode] Fixed prompts over 50,000 characters being cut off silently: the prompt now stays in the chat box with a notice, and a paste over the limit is refused with a notice
  • [VSCode] Fixed a click on the survey or "Report a problem" buttons sending the unfinished prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed cloud sessions opened from the extension's Web tab bringing back turns that /clear, or Retry or Edit of a typed prompt, had removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a deleted session's file coming back when that session was renamed in the extension
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude carrying out an unapproved plan after a window reload: a step interrupted in plan mode now stops with a notice when the session comes back in another permission mode
  • [VSCode] Improved the "not signed in" message behind a Claude apps gateway: it now looks like an error and has a Sign in link
  • [VSCode] Changed links in Claude's replies that point at Claude sign-in, connector or API addresses to show as text with the address, instead of opening in the browser
  • [VSCode] Fixed a possible chat panel freeze when a dropped item's path contains a very long run of "/" characters
  • [VSCode] Fixed the claude-vscode.toggleDictation command starting dictation in every open Claude view at once; it now acts only in the view you are using, and a second press stops it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel slowing down while a reply with many unclosed $$ math fences, each shorter than the last, streams in
  • [VSCode] Improved the chat panel's diagnostics tool for large workspaces: it leaves out files with no problems, returns compact JSON, and accepts an optional minimum severity
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed scheduled tasks silently dropping a connector named memory: runs now keep it, mounted under that name plus a short suffix
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Send now on a waiting message in cloud sessions ending running background agents; they now keep running
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the stalled-setup warning on self-hosted environments: its link now prefers your organization's default or an environment with a live runner, and names it
  • [Code Review] Changed unlinking a GitHub organization to also turn off its All repositories setting in Code Review; it stays off after you relink until you turn it back on
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag setup blocking launch when the channel list couldn't fully load; admins can now launch without picking a channel
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Claude Tag row to the Models admin page for Enterprise orgs with Claude Tag connected, linking to where its model defaults are managed
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed saving auto mode allow rules in Claude Tag admin settings overwriting another admin's changes; the save is now refused with a message
